title: The kalam cosmological argument
note: The kalam argument, from medieval Islamic theology and revived by William Lane Craig, runs: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; so the universe has a cause. Premise 2 is defended philosophically (no actual infinite, no infinite built step by step) and scientifically (Big Bang cosmology, thermodynamics).

read.title: Did the universe begin?
text: William Lane Craig's version of the kalam argument is short:
(1) Whatever begins to exist has a cause. (2) The universe began to exist. (3) Therefore, the universe has a cause.

Craig defends premise (2) in two ways. Philosophically, he argues that an actual infinite cannot exist in reality. Hilbert's Hotel, with infinitely many rooms all occupied, could still welcome new guests by shifting everyone down a room; if guests left, subtracting equal infinities could give different answers. If such absurdities rule out an actual infinite, there cannot be an infinite series of past events. And even if one could exist, it could not be formed by adding one event after another. Scientifically, Big Bang cosmology and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem point to a beginning, as does the second law of thermodynamics.
Craig then argues the cause must be uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial, and personal, since only a free agent could produce a temporal effect from a timeless state.
A standard objection targets premise (1): quantum events, such as the decay of an atom, seem to have no cause. If the micro-world allows uncaused events, why not the universe?

Craig replies that quantum events are not uncaused in the relevant sense. They occur within a physical vacuum governed by laws, which is a rich state of energy, not nothing. Coming into being from literally nothing, without any cause, he argues, is worse than magic.

q.q: What is Hilbert's Hotel used to show?
o: Actual infinites yield absurd results in reality
Hotels cannot be built in space

q.q: Which premise does the quantum objection target?
o: Whatever begins to exist has a cause

q.q: Why does Craig say quantum events are not uncaused 'from nothing'?
o: They have been shown to be illusory
They arise within a law-governed physical vacuum
They happen only at the Big Bang
